title: The Case of the Wobbly Scepter
markdown:
The Guildhall of the Luminescent Arts thrummed. Tapestries of celestial marvels watched a formal society vote. The voting urn was already in place when the trouble began. Elara the hedgehog, ceramics assistant, twitched one last quill into alignment. Her plan covered the angle of the urn, the geometry of the cucumber sandwiches, even the pens in distinct hues. Tonight they would elect a Guildmaster. Nothing, she had decided, would wobble.

Finn the stoat leaned on a velvet pillar, a sleek comma of attention. He nodded once. Elara took it as the whole speech.

The curtain was flung aside. Elder Bramble, a badger of thunderous gravitas, surveyed the cloaked assembly and beamed at the urn.

“An excellent vessel! But surely our electors require light!”

Before Elara could protest, he produced an ornate lamp from his robes and set it, with a theatrical wink, directly in front of the opening. Half the mouth of the urn went dark.

Crisis, then: her blueprint had not included a landslide of helpfulness. “My Lord Bramble,” she said, tighter than she liked, “the placement casts shadows where the ballots need to fall.”

“Nonsense! Light is paramount!”

A suppressed gasp moved the hall. Elara’s spines prickled. She did not snatch the lamp. She counted to three, which was a decision, and let the first votes begin in the half-dark rather than start a quarrel with thunder.

The ceremonial scepter waited on a plush cushion atop a plinth she had chosen for its refusal to dance. Whispers rose. Lady Seraphina the peacock swept forward like weather.

“This static display will not do!”

She whisked the scepter from its rest and began a spontaneous ballet of civic feeling, plumage a moving curtain. The lamp wobbled. The scepter missed a vase of Moonpetal blossoms by a breath that smelled of almost-disaster. Lamplight jittered on brass. Cloaked members stepped back as if the dance had voting rights. The solemn election was becoming a poorly booked revue.

Elara’s edifice of order dissolved in plumage. Voters, bemused and then audible, murmured. She nearly stepped in, nearly cited the scrolls. Finn’s silence held her for a second look: the growth she needed was not a better diagram. It was the nerve to say the obvious while people were performing.

Finn left the pillar without fuss. Whiskers ticking, he offered no repair.

“The light is very bright,” he murmured, “and the dance is spirited. No one has asked whether the scepter can be held still enough for the count.”

The worst crisis was not the lamp or the dance. It was that everyone had seen the problem and kept applauding around it.

A hush, unexpected as a dropped pin in velvet, fell. Elara stepped forward on that quiet.

“Elder Bramble. Lady Seraphina. I am grateful for the invention. For the vote to stand, the lamp must leave the urn’s mouth visible, and the scepter must go back to the plinth until the tally is done.” She looked at the room, not the trophies. “We can still do this. Quietly. Better, even.”

Elder Bramble chuckled, sheepish, and moved the lamp. Lady Seraphina, flustered into something like thought, returned the scepter. Mist went off the tension. Ballots found the opening. The rest of the count ran like a kiln with the door shut: heat, patience, no ballet.

Professor Nocturne, a wise old owl, was named Guildmaster without fanfare. Members dispersed into a warmer hall. Elara watched Finn, a small knowing at her mouth. The evening had not followed the scrolls. Admitting what they all already knew had been the only ceremony required. On the plinth the scepter sat, unmoving, catching honest light at last.
